summary.title: Microservices - Please, don't
summary.one_liner: Microservices bring hidden costs (distributed transactions, network latency, cross-team coordination, and no automatic scaling or cleanliness gains), so adopt them only once your domain, workflows, and monitoring are well understood.
takeaways: Five common beliefs about microservices (cleaner code, easier, faster, simpler for engineers, better scalability) are often false.
Splitting into services introduces distributed transactions (sagas), network I/O, and failure handling across remote calls.
A monolith can be scaled by running logical clusters that handle different workloads, such as API, front end, and background jobs.
Microservices make sense once the domain is well understood, workflows and failure paths are known, and monitoring is in place.
The author suggests building internal services as clean code modules and extracting them into separate services only when a real need arises.
summary.summary: This essay, adapted from a Boston Golang meetup lightning talk by Sean Kelly (Riak developer program), examines common assumptions behind microservice architectures. It walks through five beliefs (cleaner code, easier, faster, simpler for engineers, better scalability) and explains why each is not always true, citing distributed transactions, network overhead, I/O costs, isolated codebases, and monolith scaling. It closes with guidance on when microservices fit: a deep domain understanding, mapped workflows, solid monitoring, and a demonstrable business case. The author is not arguing microservices are bad, only that they should be adopted deliberately.
